newsitem.title: USA: Western U.S. hit by floods, evacuations.
newsitem.headline: Western U.S. hit by floods, evacuations.

text.p: Rain pounded the U.S. West coast on Thursday, pushing rivers to bursting point and causing floods and evacuations in northern California's scenic wine country and Nevada.

The relentless rains moved south, swelling rivers in central California and leaving a trail of power outages. Wind and rain persisted in Washington state, devastated by a series of punishing storms over the last week, but the state was hoping for a respite later on Thursday.
In Nevada, heavy rain caused the worst flooding in downtown Reno in more than 40 years but most casinos remained open.
At least 14 deaths are blamed on the storms, estimated to have caused up to $250 million in property damage in Washington, Oregon and northern California.
Throughout the region, torrential rains have caused mudslides, opened huge sinkholes in streets and forced the closure of countless roads, making travel hazardous.

Oregon Gov. John Kitzhaber declared emergencies in five counties because of the storms and mobilized 200 National Guard troops to help with transportation, traffic control and sandbagging. Gov. Mike Lowry has declared a state of emergency in 19 Washington counties.

In northern California's wine country, the Russian River burst its banks, inundating the town of Guerneville and other low-lying areas with muddy brown water. Homes and businesses in Guerneville, 50 miles (80 kms) north of San Francisco, were flooded and the town was cut off.
Residents hurriedly threw possessions into bags as the river rose on Wednesday and some stranded people had to be rescued by National Guard helicopters.
About 175 evacuees spent the night at a Red Cross shelter in nearby Sebastopol, Janice Atkinson, a spokeswoman for the Sonoma County Office of Emergency Services, said.
The Russian River was holding at around its crest level, about 11 ft (3.3 metres) above flood stage, on Thursday morning, but officials hoped the river would start to recede later in the day.
But Atkinson said evacuated residents should not think they would be able to return home on Thursday. "It's not going to happen. It's got to go down quite a way before roads reopen," she said.

The nearby Napa River in northern California crested at 3 feet (one metre) above flood stage near St. Helena late on Wednesday, turning vineyards into huge lakes and forcing evacuations. But a flood warning for the Napa River was canceled on Thursday morning.

The National Weather Service issued a flash flood warning for most counties in the San Francisco Bay area. A flood watch was issued for the Pajaro River in central California which rose quickly because of heavy rain.

About 19,000 homes and business in northern and central California were without electricity because of the storm, Pacific Gas and Electric Co. spokesman Greg Pruett said. Since New Year's Eve, almost 200,000 PG&E customers had suffered power cuts at some time, he said.
In the area around Seattle, 13,600 customers remained cut off, down from a peak of 113,000 from the latest storm, Puget Sound Power and Light Co., said.

In Seattle, mudslides forced the evacuation of more than 40 homes -- many valued at well over $1 million -- overlooking Puget Sound in the city's exclusive Magnolia section. Several homes sustained serious damage.
A yawning sinkhole more than 150 feet (45 metres) wide swallowed a car and forced several evacuations in the Seattle suburb of Shoreline, where another sinkhole destroyed a gas station.
In Oregon, floodwaters shut off access to downtown Tualatin south of Portland, and the posh suburb of Lake Oswego, hard hit by a flood last February, once again was threatened by rising waters.
